title: Does Muon Need Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping?

paper.title: Does Muon Need Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Muon combines current and past gradients into matrix momentum. For M = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ M=U\Sigma V^{\top} , the idealized polar update Q = U ​ V ⊤ Q=UV^{\top} gives every singular direction the same weight. We refer to this as the flat profile. Several recent optimizers replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that give each direction its own gain. We ask how much of this spectral detail a Muon update needs . Our spectral diagnostics show that approximately 94 94 – 97 % 97\% of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with
a reference gradient. We introduce BulkBoost , a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants. The latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko–Pastur reference edge for Muon ’s Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from the spikes above it. Both variants increase the bulk’s relative weight through one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix’s unreweighted direction. For a fixed partition, our theory gives the first-order condition under which moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss. It also quantifies the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate, over all per-mode reallocations, that two bands can capture. A polar-plus-low-rank representation enables an approximation without a full SVD, tracking only the spike subspace. Across 30 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia- 14 14 M to 410 410 M and
six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with the fine-grained
power-law profile of Freon ( Shumaylov et al., 2026 ) and outperforms Spectra ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Measured against Muon ’s flat profile, Freon reduces final
loss by 0.022 % 0.022\% of the pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of 0.073 0.073 – 0.147 % 0.147\% . These observations suggest that useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: An optimizer for neural-network weight matrices decides two things: how large an update is, and how the update is spread across directions. Muon , an optimizer for language-model training, combines current and past gradients into a matrix momentum M M ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its SVD, M = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ M=U\Sigma V^{\top} , writes M M as a sum of orthogonal directions weighted by their singular values. The idealized polar update Q = U ​ V ⊤ Q=UV^{\top} keeps these directions but sets every singular value to one . Each direction therefore receives the same gain. We refer to this as the flat profile . Recent optimizers depart from this flat profile through spectral maps U ​ g ​ ( Σ ) ​ V ⊤ Ug(\Sigma)V^{\top} , where the gain varies across singular directions ( Shumaylov et al., 2026 ; Dong & Sawin, 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Pang et al., 2026 ; Feoktistov et al., 2026 ) . At the same time, Shumaylov et al. (2026) show that substantially different spectra, including random and inverted ones, can remain effective. These results raise a more basic question than which detailed profile is best: does Muon need fine-grained spectral shaping, or is a coarse reallocation between two groups of directions enough? Two observations motivate this question. First, a direction’s strength in the sampled momentum, its separation from sampling noise, and the benefit of increasing its update weight are distinct quantities. A small singular value can still carry signal, and a large one need not deserve more weight. Second, our diagnostics reveal a broad spectral bulk and a small leading band. Under a Gaussian white-noise reference model, random matrix theory provides an asymptotic upper spectral edge, the noise edge ( Marchenko & Pastur, 1967 ; Baik et al., 2005 ; Benaych-Georges & Nadakuditi, 2012 ) . We call directions above this reference edge spikes and the remaining directions the bulk . On Pythia-70M Muon trajectories, approximately 93.7 93.7 – 97.1 % 97.1\% of pooled singular modes lie in the bulk (Appendix D ). These below-edge singular modes, the bulk , are weak individually, yet their aggregate signed alignment with an independently sampled reference gradient is positive in every analyzed matrix. Thus, the broad spectral bulk makes a non-negligible collective contribution even though its individual directions are weak. These measurements motivate a two-band partition. We introduce BulkBoost , whose exact target reweights Muon ’s polar direction in two bands. The spike and bulk gains are 1 1 and ρ \rho before normalization, and the update is then rescaled to keep the Frobenius norm of the unreweighted direction. At the exact-target level, ρ = 1 \rho=1 recovers Q Q , while ρ > 1 \rho>1 increases the bulk’s relative weight. Once the partition is chosen, the same ρ \rho controls reallocation across all spectrally updated matrices. We consider two rules for the split. The fixed-rank rule , BB-Static , takes a prescribed fraction p p of the leading directions, shared across matrices and held fixed within each run. Our shared configuration uses p = 5 % p=5\% , within the pooled spike fraction of 2.9 2.9 – 6.3 % 6.3\% measured in our diagnostics (Appendix D ). We also test smaller and larger fractions. The noise-calibrated rule , BB-Adaptive , estimates the sampling noise from two minibatch halves, propagates it through the momentum, and places the split at the resulting noise edge for each matrix and step. The edge assumes isotropic Gaussian noise. Since the real gradient noise is not isotropic, this split is an approximation. Our contributions are as follows. 1. A two-band reweighting rule. BulkBoost reweights Muon ’s flat update in two bands with one shared gain. The split between the bands comes either from a fixed fraction of directions or from a noise-calibrated edge. An exact polar-plus-low-rank identity lets us avoid a full SVD (Section 3 ). 2. What the two bands capture. For a fixed partition, we characterize to first order when shifting weight toward the bulk lowers the loss, and how much of the best per-direction improvement two bands can reach (Section 4 ). 3. Evidence from the spectrum. Our spectral diagnostics establish that most singular directions of Muon ’s momentum lie below the noise edge. This bulk is weak direction by direction, yet it carries useful signal in aggregate. Giving it more relative weight lowers the loss after a single update in most tested states (Appendices D and E.2 ). 4. Competitive gains without fine-grained shaping. In continued pretraining settings spanning Pythia- 14 14 M to 410 410 M and six corpora, two-band reweighting gives, on average, a slightly larger improvement over Muon ’s flat profile than the fine-grained direction-specific spectral profiles we compare against. Thus, a single shared gain between spikes and bulk is enough in these settings (Section 5 ). Related work is provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4 Theory of Two-Band Reweighting
sections.text: We first give a first-order test for when two-band reweighting lowers the loss, and quantify how much of the best per-direction improvement two bands can capture. We then give the exact structure behind the SVD-free realization.

Its first-order rate is therefore at most ‖ u ⟂ ‖ 2 \|u_{\perp}\|_{2} . Finer shaping can thus add at most the share 1 − R bt 1-R_{\mathrm{bt}} , which comes from utility differences within the bands. The split rule, whether the noise edge or a fixed fraction, only decides which directions fall in each band. The sign of Δ \Delta and the size of R bt R_{\mathrm{bt}} depend on the utilities. When Δ > 0 \Delta>0 , small enough increases in ρ \rho lower the loss. The theorem does not say how large ρ \rho may be, so it does not justify a specific finite gain such as ρ = 4 \rho=4 . Here, first order refers to small changes in the gains; the parameter update itself is a finite step. With one ρ \rho shared by all matrices, each norm-matched separately, the rates from Theorem 1 (i) add up across matrices under joint differentiability (Appendix E.2 ). Appendices E.2 and G.2 test finite values of ρ \rho . Appendix F.1 gives the proof.

sections.text: A shared bulk gain also gives the update a simple form. The polar factor carries the bulk, and only a correction in the spike subspace remains. The squared Frobenius norm of D ~ ​ ( a , ρ ) \widetilde{D}(a,\rho) is ‖ a ‖ 2 2 + ρ 2 ​ ( d − r ) \|a\|_{2}^{2}+\rho^{2}(d-r) , so for a = 𝟏 r a=\mathbf{1}_{r} the normalizer c ρ , r c_{\rho,r} restores ‖ Q ‖ F = d \|Q\|_{F}=\sqrt{d} (Corollary 3 ). sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: This section tests whether two bands are enough in practice. The diagnostics in Appendix D motivate this test. On Pythia-70M Muon trajectories, 94–97% of singular directions lie below the noise edge, and this bulk is weak per direction but positively aligned with a reference gradient in aggregate. We compare both BulkBoost variants, BB-Static and BB-Adaptive , with Muon ’s flat profile and with fine-grained spectral profiles in continued pretraining. We also compare the two variants with each other. Extended results appear in Appendix G . Figure 1: Held-out loss versus training tokens on Wiki-zh, one column per model scale. Top: the full run, with the pre-adaptation loss ℓ 0 \ell_{0} dotted and the zoomed interval shaded. Bottom: the shaded interval at a finer vertical scale. The BB-Static curve uses p = 1.5 % p=1.5\% , the leading fraction of Spectra , so the two can be compared directly. Appendix G.3 shows the other corpora. BulkBoost configurations. Unless varied in an ablation, both variants use ρ = 4 \rho=4 , Q ^ t = PolarExpress ⁡ ( M t ) \widehat{Q}_{t}=\operatorname{PolarExpress}(M_{t}) ( Amsel et al., 2026a ) , q = 6 q=6 warm-started block iterations for spike tracking, and the norm matching in equation 12 . Like Newton–Schulz, Polar Express uses only matrix products. It approximates the polar factor more closely, which the correction in equation 11 needs. Muon and both variants use Nesterov momentum β = 0.95 \beta=0.95 . BB-Adaptive splits at τ ^ t \widehat{\tau}_{t} (Section 3.1 ) with γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 , κ edge = 1 \kappa_{\mathrm{edge}}=1 , and the rank cap of Appendix C.3 . BB-Static keeps r t = ⌈ p ​ d ⌉ r_{t}=\lceil pd\rceil spike directions, with one fraction p p for all matrices and the whole run. We test p ∈ { 0.015 , 0.02 , 0.05 , 0.15 , 0.20 } p\in\{0.015,0.02,0.05,0.15,0.20\} (Table 9 ). Our shared configuration, BB-Static (5%) , uses p = 5 % p=5\% , which lies within the 2.9–6.3% spike fraction measured in Appendix D . BB-Static † instead reports, for each setting, the fraction with the lowest mean final held-out loss. Because this choice uses the reported loss, BB-Static † shows what per-setting tuning can reach. Compared methods. We compare both BulkBoost variants with five baselines. Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) approximates the flat profile with Newton–Schulz iterations and is the reference for all relative comparisons. Two baselines use fine-grained spectral profiles. Freon ( Shumaylov et al., 2026 ) uses a power-law profile with c = 0.667 c=0.667 ; c = 1 2 c=\tfrac{1}{2} recovers the flat profile. Spectra ( Huang et al., 2026 ) rescales the leading singular values to the root-mean-square level of the tail. It keeps the tail’s unequal singular values, whereas BulkBoost gives the whole bulk one gain. We use its recommended leading fraction of 1.5%. We also run BB-Static at p = 1.5 % p=1.5\% , so the two methods can be compared with the same number of spike directions (Figure 1 ). The other two baselines are AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017 ) and DeVA ( Song et al., 2026 ) , which separates variance adaptation from scale-invariant matrix updates. Models and datasets. We continue pretraining converged Pythia checkpoints ( Biderman et al., 2023 ) at five scales, 14M, 31M, 70M, 160M, and 410M, on six corpora: math (FineMath-4, FineMath-3), Code (CodeParrot), and multilingual text (Wiki-de, Wiki-zh, Wiki-ar). See Appendix G.1 . Token sampling and evaluation. Each corpus is tokenized once with Pythia’s GPT-NeoX tokenizer, so all scales and methods reuse the same tokenized data. We reserve the first 1 1 M tokens for held-out evaluation and train on the remainder. Training samples uniformly random contiguous 1024 1024 -token windows with a run-specific seed. A run takes 3,051 3,051 steps of 32 32 sequences ( 32,768 32,768 tokens per step), or about 100 100 M tokens, with a cosine learning-rate schedule. Every 100 100 steps, we evaluate on 128 128 deterministic, evenly spaced held-out windows, shared across steps and methods. The main comparisons use three seeds. Pre-adaptation loss. For each model–corpus pair, let ℓ 0 \ell_{0} and ℓ final \ell_{\mathrm{final}} denote the held-out losses before and after continued pretraining, and define Δ = ℓ final − ℓ 0 \Delta=\ell_{\mathrm{final}}-\ell_{0} . All methods start from the same pretrained checkpoint and are evaluated on the same held-out windows. We report loss differences between methods as a percentage of ℓ 0 \ell_{0} . Table 8 in Appendix G.1 reports ℓ 0 \ell_{0} and Δ \Delta for Muon . Learning-rate calibration. We tune one learning rate per model scale on FineMath-4 and reuse it for every method and all six corpora. To choose it, we run a short learning-rate sweep over multiples of a reference rate, which is 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Pythia-14M, 31M, and 70M and 10 − 3 10^{-3} for 160M and 410M. The multipliers are { 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 } \{0.01,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2,4\} . Each sweep run trains one method for 20M tokens with one seed, and we record its final validation loss. The sweep covers every method except AdamW 1 1 1 Because Pythia models are trained with AdamW and their learning rate decays to 0.1 × 0.1\times the base rate at convergence, we omit AdamW from the sweep. . In it, BB-Static uses p = 20 % p=20\% , and both BulkBoost variants use ρ = 4 \rho=4 . At each scale, we then fix one shared multiplier: the one that is best for most swept methods. It is 0.1 × 0.1\times for 14M, 31M, and 160M, 0.25 × 0.25\times for 70M, and 0.05 × 0.05\times for 410M. The resulting peak learning rates are 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} for 14M and 31M, 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for 70M, 10 − 4 10^{-4} for 160M, and 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} for 410M. For every swept method, the shared multiplier is also its own best, with two exceptions. At 70M, Muon does best at 0.1 × 0.1\times ( 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} ), with a sweep loss of 2.779 2.779 against 2.783 2.783 at the shared 0.25 × 0.25\times . Its loss then jumps to 2.919 2.919 at the next multiplier, 0.5 × 0.5\times , so the shared rate stays in Muon ’s near-optimal range. At 160M, Spectra does best at 0.05 × 0.05\times ( 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} ), with a sweep loss of 2.552 2.552 against 2.553 2.553 at the shared 0.1 × 0.1\times . Figure 2 and Table 11 in Appendix G.2 report the full sweep. Shared rate in the 100M-token runs. Every 100M-token run uses the shared rate of its scale, with no further tuning. This includes AdamW , which the sweep does not cover. It also includes all five BB-Static fractions in Table 9 , so BB-Static (5%) and BB-Static † use it too. Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 1 report these runs.

Δ \Delta vs. Muon : the loss difference from Muon as a percentage of ℓ 0 \ell_{0} , averaged over settings within each seed. We report the mean ± \pm std dev of the three seed averages. Negative values favor the method. Tokens saved : the mean and median share of the 100M-token budget saved in reaching Muon ’s final loss, over the winning settings and the seeds that end below Muon (Table 10 ). Two bands match or beat fine-grained profiles. Measured against Muon ’s flat profile, BB-Static (5%) , BB-Adaptive , and BB-Static † lower the final loss in 23 23 , 24 24 , and 25 25 of the 30 30 settings, by 0.073 % 0.073\% , 0.077 % 0.077\% , and 0.147 % 0.147\% of ℓ 0 \ell_{0} on average (Table 2 ). The fine-grained Freon does so in 19 19 settings, by 0.022 % 0.022\% . BB-Static (5%) beats Freon in 13 13 settings and loses in 13 13 , and BB-Adaptive beats it in 17 17 and loses in 10 10 . Spectra and DeVA trail Muon in all 30 30 settings, and every BulkBoost configuration beats both. This includes BB-Static at Spectra ’s leading fraction of 1.5 % 1.5\% (Table 9 ). The original DeVA and Spectra studies pretrain from scratch ( Song et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , which differs from our continued pretraining setup. These results suggest that a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles. Static and adaptive splits. BB-Static † beats BB-Adaptive in 20 20 settings and loses in 4 4 , but it selects its fraction on the reported loss. Without any fraction search, BB-Adaptive matches BB-Static (5%) , with 10 10 wins, 6 6 losses, and 14 14 ties. Token efficiency and runtime trade-offs. Among settings where it outperforms Muon , BB-Adaptive reaches Muon ’s final loss using 7.99 % 7.99\% fewer tokens on average, with a median saving of 8.01 % 8.01\% (Table 2 ). The extensively tuned BB-Static † increases these savings to 10 % 10\% and 10.28 % 10.28\% , respectively. These token savings come with additional per-step computation. At 70M–410M, measured per-step runtimes are 1.36 1.36 – 1.50 × 1.50\times Muon ’s for BB-Adaptive , compared with 1.19 1.19 – 1.27 × 1.27\times for the measured static configurations (Appendix G ). Adaptive selection avoids fraction search, while static selection offers cheaper execution once a suitable fraction is identified. Neither DeVA nor Spectra achieves lower mean final validation loss than Muon in any of the 30 30 settings (Table 1 ); their token-saving averages over wins are therefore undefined (“–” in Table 2 ). DeVA outperforms AdamW in 18 18 settings and trails it in 12 12 . Table 10 in Appendix G.2 identifies the winning model–corpus settings and reports their token savings and variation across seeds. Ablations. Appendix G.2 compares the static and adaptive splits, sweeps the gain ρ \rho , and shows that a third band does not improve on two. In exact-SVD single-update tests on Pythia-70M, ρ = 1.25 \rho=1.25 and 1.5 1.5 lower the loss relative to the flat update ( ρ = 1 \rho=1 ) in five of six settings (Appendix E.2 ). Conclusion. Our diagnostics reveal that Muon ’s momentum has a broad spectral bulk whose individual directions are weak but collectively aligned with a reference gradient. BulkBoost exploits this structure with only two bands and a single shared bulk-to-spike gain. Our theory shows when this coarse reallocation is locally beneficial and what finer shaping can add through within-band variation. An exact polar-plus-low-rank identity enables an SVD-free realization. Across 30 30 continued-pretraining settings, the two-band variants match or exceed the finer spectral baselines in aggregate. Single-update experiments show that bulk emphasis lowers the loss relative to the exact flat update in five of six states. Together, these results suggest that useful departures from Muon ’s flat spectrum can be surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain can capture at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles . Limitations. The strongest BB-Static results select the fraction separately for each setting. A shared fraction avoids this search, but the best fraction varies across settings (Table 9 ). BB-Adaptive instead sets the split online from the noise edge. It needs no fraction search, but it costs more per step. The noise edge comes from a white Gaussian noise reference model, so it separates signal from noise only approximately. Our evaluation is restricted to Pythia continued pretraining under the reported tuning protocol. Extending the evaluation to other architectures and training regimes remains future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: We position BulkBoost within matrix-aware optimization, spectral reweighting, and subspace selection. Our focus is the allocation of a fixed per-matrix direction norm between two spectral bands, separating partition selection –by fixed rank or a noise-calibrated edge–from the relative gain assigned to the bulk.

sections.heading: A.1 Matrix-Aware Optimization and Spectral Geometry
sections.text: Stochastic spectral descent exploits matrix geometry rather than treating a parameter matrix as an unstructured vector ( Carlson et al., 2015 ) . Bernstein & Newhouse (2024) organize several optimizer constructions through norm-constrained steepest descent. Muon applies an approximate polar map to matrix momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) ; its large-scale realization addresses update scaling, weight decay, and distributed execution for language-model training ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Scion develops a broader family of norm-constrained linear minimization oracles ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , while PolarGrad places polar-based updates within a matrix-aware preconditioning framework ( Lau et al., 2025 ) . These perspectives distinguish the geometry defining an update from its scalar normalization. Within this setting, BulkBoost ’s exact target retains the singular frame of M t M_{t} and reallocates gains between two bands while preserving the Frobenius norm of its polar factor Q t Q_{t} . A related line uses accumulated gradient statistics for matrix preconditioning. Shampoo constructs tensor-structured preconditioners ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; SOAP performs Adam-style adaptation in Shampoo’s eigenbasis ( Vyas et al., 2024 ) . DeVA separates variance adaptation from scale-invariant vector and matrix update rules ( Song et al., 2026 ) . COSMOS combines SOAP-style adaptation in a leading eigensubspace with Muon on its complement ( Liming Liu et al., 2026 ) , illustrating the use of distinct optimization rules in different spectral subspaces. BulkBoost instead applies one norm-matched reweighting rule with a common gain within each band. Its noise-calibrated variant uses split-minibatch statistics to select band membership, not to assign direction-specific second-moment gains; its fixed-rank variant requires no noise estimate.

sections.heading: A.2 Spectral Shaping Beyond Muon ’s Flat Profile
sections.text: Several recent studies replace Muon ’s equal-gain profile with a nonconstant spectral map. Shumaylov et al. (2026) show that random and inverted spectra can remain effective and introduce Freon through a family of Schatten-based update rules. Muon p uses fractional spectral powers ( Dong & Sawin, 2026 ) , while DynMuon varies the shaping profile over training ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . HTMuon uses heavy-tailed spectral correction ( Pang et al., 2026 ) , and Softsign introduces smooth alternatives to sign updates, including the matrix optimizer SoftMuon ( Feoktistov et al., 2026 ) . These studies show that exact spectral flattening is one effective allocation rather than a necessary choice. Spectral clipping provides another alternative. The Spectra framework of Jiang et al. (2026) studies clipping before and after preconditioning, with efficient soft spectral clipping via Newton–Schulz iterations. Musec replaces full flattening with momentum spectral clipping and implements smooth saturation using coupled iterations ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . These approaches retain or modify variation along the spectrum. BulkBoost instead asks whether useful reallocation can be captured by a norm-matched two-band profile, without fine-grained spectral shaping. Its exact target assigns equal gains within each band, with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated rules determining band membership separately from the relative bulk-to-spike gain.

sections.heading: A.3 Head–Bulk Allocation and the Closest Related Methods
sections.text: The Spectra optimizer of Huang et al. (2026) is distinct from the similarly named Spectra framework of Jiang et al. (2026) . It tracks a leading momentum subspace, replaces its singular values with a tail-scale estimate, and retains the residual tail before RMS-normalizing the update. Its leading-subspace intervention and warm-started iteration are closely related to our construction. The central difference is the reference spectrum: Spectra retains the raw tail’s unequal singular magnitudes, whereas BulkBoost ’s exact target reweights the polar factor Q t Q_{t} with equal gains within each band. Both fixed-rank and noise-calibrated BulkBoost use this two-level rule, differing in band selection. Under norm matching, relative head suppression and relative bulk emphasis are not opposite reallocations. The meaningful distinctions are the underlying spectral profile, partition rule, and normalization, rather than the terminology of suppression versus amplification.

sections.heading: A.4 Random-Matrix Noise Edges and Spectral Estimation
sections.text: The Marchenko–Pastur law describes the limiting spectrum of appropriate random covariance matrices ( Marchenko & Pastur, 1967 ) . Spiked-model theory characterizes transitions in leading empirical eigenvalues ( Baik et al., 2005 ) , while rectangular perturbation theory analyzes singular values and singular-vector alignment ( Benaych-Georges & Nadakuditi, 2012 ) . Optimal singular-value shrinkage studies reconstruction of an underlying matrix under specified noise and loss models ( Gavish & Donoho, 2017 ) . These results provide statistical reference scales and estimation criteria, but do not determine which spectral allocation best reduces evaluation loss after an optimizer update. Gradient-noise measurements have also been used to characterize useful batch sizes and training efficiency ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) . The noise-calibrated variant of BulkBoost uses split-minibatch differences to estimate the raw full-minibatch noise variance. It rescales this estimate by the squared global clipping factor before smoothing and uses the reference-model Nesterov correction to calibrate an edge for M t M_{t} (Section 3.1 ). The resulting white-noise reference selects band membership; the relative gain ρ \rho remains a separate optimization choice. The edge is neither an exact signal–noise separator nor a prescription to discard below-edge modes. The fixed-rank variant selects its partition without estimating a noise edge.

sections.heading: A.5 Polar Computation, Subspace Tracking, and Low-Rank Updates
sections.text: Iterative polar decomposition has a classical numerical foundation ( Higham, 1986 ) . Polar Express develops optimized matrix-sign iterations and their use in Muon ( Amsel et al., 2026a ) . Randomized range finding and subspace iteration provide standard tools for estimating leading singular spaces without a full decomposition ( Halko et al., 2011 ) . Spectral scaling measurements further highlight the role of finite-iteration accuracy: momentum singular-value quantiles vary with layer and model scale, affecting which tail directions Newton–Schulz iterations resolve ( Magakyan et al., 2026 ) . Our realization combines Muon ’s numerical polar approximation Q ^ t \widehat{Q}_{t} with warm-started block iteration to approximate the selected spike subspace. The noise-calibrated tracker augments the retained basis with fresh probes, whereas fixed-rank tracking uses a block of prescribed width. Neither construction explicitly computes individual bulk singular vectors. The shared bulk gain determines how these numerical ingredients combine into the prescribed reweighted target. Low-rank optimization methods address related computational objectives. GaLore projects gradients to reduce optimizer-state memory ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , while Dion uses distributed, amortized low-rank orthonormalized updates with error feedback ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Dion3 combines algorithmic and systems techniques for efficient orthogonal updates ( Amsel et al., 2026b ) . In BulkBoost , the low-rank object is instead a correction to a scaled polar update (Theorem 2 ). For full-rank M t M_{t} and ρ > 0 \rho>0 , the exact two-level target remains full rank; only its correction is confined to the selected spike subspace. The numerical realization matches ‖ Q ^ t ‖ F \|\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F} , rather than imposing the exact-polar norm d \sqrt{d} . Its tracking cost depends on the trial-space width and iteration count as well as the retained rank, so avoiding an explicit SVD does not by itself establish a runtime advantage.

sections.heading: A.6 Curvature, Noise Geometry, and Continuation Utility
sections.text: Pre-update gradient alignment captures only part of update quality. Wang et al. (2026) study Muon ’s advantage through directional curvature, distinguishing first-order gain from the second-order penalty. Quadratic Spectral Descent incorporates a quadratic surrogate under a spectral-norm constraint ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while Beneventano et al. (2026) analyze spectral dynamics and noise geometry under Muon . These studies complement spectral-allocation comparisons by examining how curvature and transformed noise affect optimization, beyond singular magnitudes alone. Differentiating evaluation loss through training has a history in hyperparameter optimization and bilevel learning ( Maclaurin et al., 2015 ; Franceschi et al., 2018 ) . Our continuation utility applies this sensitivity viewpoint to a fixed-frame spectral intervention: it is the negative derivative of post-update or later evaluation loss with respect to a current applied singular-direction gain, evaluated at Muon ’s equal-gain allocation. Subsequent training follows a fixed policy, while gradients and optimizer states can respond to the intervention. For either fixed-rank or noise-calibrated band selection, Theorem 1 characterizes local allocation preferences and the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate accessible to two bands under norm matching. This is an analysis of the exact spectral target, not an online hypergradient procedure for selecting ρ \rho . Recent work on optimizer-memory schedules further emphasizes the roles of training horizon and memory timescale in optimizer comparisons ( Everett & Qiu, 2026 ) . Our pre-update alignment diagnostics, single-update loss measurements, and continued-pretraining experiments examine distinct aspects of spectral allocation: immediate alignment, the loss response to a current intervention, and performance over a training run.

sections.heading: A.7 Controlled Continued-Pretraining Evaluation
sections.text: Pythia provides a public model suite designed for analysis across training and scale ( Biderman et al., 2023 ) . Continued pretraining on domains and tasks is an established adaptation setting ( Gururangan et al., 2020 ) . We use this setting to compare fixed-rank and noise-calibrated spectral reweighting from common pretrained checkpoints, under matched training-token budgets and a common validation protocol. This complements the from-scratch language-model training settings used by several related optimizers and evaluates both allocation and partition-selection rules during adaptation. Our comparisons distinguish validation loss and token efficiency from per-step computation and fraction-selection effort (Section 5 ).

sections.text: This appendix supplements Section 2 with normalization identities, gain diagnostics, and rank conventions, and derives the numerical norm matching used in Section 3 .

sections.heading: Normalization identity.
sections.text: For the full-rank spectral input M t = U t ​ Σ t ​ V t ⊤ M_{t}=U_{t}\Sigma_{t}V_{t}^{\top} , the rank-one singular modes are Frobenius-orthonormal: ⟨ u t , i v t , i ⊤ , u t , j v t , j ⊤ ⟩ F = ( u t , i ⊤ u t , j ) ( v t , i ⊤ v t , j ) = 𝟏 { i = j } . \left\langle u_{t,i}v_{t,i}^{\top},\,u_{t,j}v_{t,j}^{\top}\right\rangle_{F}=(u_{t,i}^{\top}u_{t,j})(v_{t,i}^{\top}v_{t,j})=\mathbf{1}\{i=j\}. The normalizer c t ​ ( w t ) c_{t}(w_{t}) therefore gives ‖ D t ​ ( w t ) ‖ F = d = ‖ Q t ‖ F \|D_{t}(w_{t})\|_{F}=\sqrt{d}=\|Q_{t}\|_{F} . The applied gain vector is c t ​ ( w t ) ​ w t c_{t}(w_{t})w_{t} , denoted by w w in Section 4.1 . For either partition, the two-level profile satisfies ∑ i = 1 d ( w t , i ( ρ ) ) 2 = r t + ρ 2 ​ ( d − r t ) , \sum_{i=1}^{d}\bigl(w_{t,i}^{(\rho)}\bigr)^{2}=r_{t}+\rho^{2}(d-r_{t}), yielding c t ​ ( w t ( ρ ) ) = c ρ , r t c_{t}(w_{t}^{(\rho)})=c_{\rho,r_{t}} whenever the profile is nonzero. For the noise-calibrated partition, the notation w t ( ρ , τ t ) w_{t}^{(\rho,\tau_{t})} makes the threshold dependence explicit. For a scalar-induced profile w t , i = g ⁡ ( σ t , i ) w_{t,i}=g(\sigma_{t,i}) , the equivalent matrix-function notation is g ⁡ ( Σ t ) = diag ⁡ ( g ⁡ ( σ t , 1 ) , … , g ⁡ ( σ t , d ) ) , D t ​ ( g ) = c t ​ ( g ) ​ U t ​ g ​ ( Σ t ) ​ V t ⊤ , g(\Sigma_{t})=\operatorname{diag}(g(\sigma_{t,1}),\ldots,g(\sigma_{t,d})),\qquad D_{t}(g)=c_{t}(g)U_{t}g(\Sigma_{t})V_{t}^{\top}, where c t ​ ( g ) = c t ​ ( w t ) c_{t}(g)=c_{t}(w_{t}) and the induced profile is nonzero.

sections.heading: Absolute gains under a relative reallocation.
sections.text: For a full-rank input with both bands nonempty, let q t = r t / d ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) q_{t}=r_{t}/d\in(0,1) denote the spike fraction. For BB-Static , q t = ⌈ p ​ d ⌉ / d q_{t}=\lceil pd\rceil/d , which can differ slightly from p p because of rounding. The applied gains relative to the flat profile are g sp = c ρ , r t = 1 q t + ρ 2 ​ ( 1 − q t ) , g bu = ρ ​ g sp . g_{\mathrm{sp}}=c_{\rho,r_{t}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{t}+\rho^{2}(1-q_{t})}},\qquad g_{\mathrm{bu}}=\rho g_{\mathrm{sp}}. (15) At fixed q t q_{t} , increasing ρ \rho above 1 1 raises g bu g_{\mathrm{bu}} toward 1 / 1 − q t 1/\sqrt{1-q_{t}} and lowers g sp g_{\mathrm{sp}} toward zero. For a small spike fraction, the bulk gain therefore stays close to one, while the spike gain can fall substantially. With q t = 0.05 q_{t}=0.05 and ρ = 4 \rho=4 , g bu ≈ 1.02 g_{\mathrm{bu}}\approx 1.02 and g sp ≈ 0.26 g_{\mathrm{sp}}\approx 0.26 . At the largest tested fraction, q t = 0.2 q_{t}=0.2 , the same ρ \rho gives g bu ≈ 1.11 g_{\mathrm{bu}}\approx 1.11 and g sp ≈ 0.28 g_{\mathrm{sp}}\approx 0.28 . Thus ρ \rho sets only the ratio of the two gains, and the absolute bulk gain changes much less than ρ \rho . More generally, multiplying every unnormalized gain by the same positive scalar leaves the norm-matched direction unchanged. For ρ > 0 \rho>0 , profiles with spike and bulk gains ( 1 , ρ ) (1,\rho) and ( 1 / ρ , 1 ) (1/\rho,1) therefore give the same update. Relative bulk emphasis and relative spike suppression describe the same norm-matched reallocation.

sections.heading: Effective bulk-to-spike gain.
sections.text: For a general spectral profile, define the ratio of root-mean-square gains across the selected bands by ρ eff ​ ( w t , ℐ sp , t ) = 1 d − r t ​ ∑ i ∈ ℐ bu , t w t , i 2 1 r t ​ ∑ i ∈ ℐ sp , t w t , i 2 . \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}(w_{t};\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{sp},t})=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{d-r_{t}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{bu},t}}w_{t,i}^{2}}{\frac{1}{r_{t}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{sp},t}}w_{t,i}^{2}}}. (16) This statistic is defined when both bands are nonempty and the denominator is positive. The common normalizer cancels, so the statistic is the same for w t w_{t} and its applied gains c t ​ ( w t ) ​ w t c_{t}(w_{t})w_{t} . In particular, the exact two-level target satisfies ρ eff = ρ \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}=\rho . For BB-Adaptive , we abbreviate it as ρ eff ​ ( w t , τ t ) \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}(w_{t};\tau_{t}) . The partition specifies band membership, whereas ρ eff \rho_{\mathrm{eff}} summarizes the relative allocation; it does not describe gain variation within a band or measure subspace-recovery accuracy.

sections.heading: Empty bands.
sections.text: For a full-rank input, reallocation between bands requires 0 < r t < d 0<r_{t}<d . If r t = d r_{t}=d , all unnormalized gains equal one and the target is Q t Q_{t} . If r t = 0 r_{t}=0 and ρ > 0 \rho>0 , all unnormalized gains equal ρ \rho , and normalization again gives Q t Q_{t} . When r t = 0 r_{t}=0 and ρ = 0 \rho=0 , the profile is zero and cannot be normalized to d \sqrt{d} . This case is excluded by the nonzero-profile condition in Section 2 .

sections.heading: Rank-deficient inputs.
sections.text: For a rank-deficient spectral input, restrict the exact construction to the active indices ℐ + , t = { i ∈ [ d ] : σ t , i > 0 } \mathcal{I}_{+,t}=\{i\in[d]:\sigma_{t,i}>0\} , with active rank d t + = | ℐ + , t | d_{t}^{+}=|\mathcal{I}_{+,t}| . The partial polar factor is Q t = ∑ i ∈ ℐ + , t u t , i ​ v t , i ⊤ , ‖ Q t ‖ F = d t + . Q_{t}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{+,t}}u_{t,i}v_{t,i}^{\top},\qquad\|Q_{t}\|_{F}=\sqrt{d_{t}^{+}}. Intersect each partition from Section 2 with ℐ + , t \mathcal{I}_{+,t} , and let r t r_{t} count the selected active spike modes. In particular, the fixed-rank rule gives r t = min ⁡ { ⌈ p ​ d ⌉ , d t + } r_{t}=\min\{\lceil pd\rceil,d_{t}^{+}\} : the prescribed fraction still refers to d = min ⁡ { m , n } d=\min\{m,n\} , while zero singular modes receive no gains. For d t + > 0 d_{t}^{+}>0 and a nonzero active gain vector, the exact normalizers are c t ​ ( w t ) = d t + ∑ i ∈ ℐ + , t w t , i 2 , c ρ , r t = d t + r t + ρ 2 ​ ( d t + − r t ) . c_{t}(w_{t})=\sqrt{\frac{d_{t}^{+}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{+,t}}w_{t,i}^{2}}},\qquad c_{\rho,r_{t}}=\sqrt{\frac{d_{t}^{+}}{r_{t}+\rho^{2}(d_{t}^{+}-r_{t})}}. The gain diagnostics in Appendix B.2 likewise use the active band sizes. The matrix dimensions remain m , n m,n ; replacing d d by d t + d_{t}^{+} in these identities does not change the dimensions used to calibrate the noise edge. For a zero spectral input, the partial polar factor and exact update are zero, without evaluating normalization ratios.

sections.heading: B.4 Derivation of Numerical Norm Matching
sections.text: The numerical update in equation 11 and equation 12 uses an approximate polar factor Q ^ t \widehat{Q}_{t} and a tracked basis X t ∈ ℝ d × r ^ t X_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\widehat{r}_{t}} . We first derive the identities in exact arithmetic, assuming that X t X_{t} has orthonormal columns; neither an exact polar factor nor exact spike recovery is required for the projection calculation. Define Q ^ sp , t = { X t ​ ( X t ⊤ ​ Q ^ t ) , m ≤ n , ( Q ^ t ​ X t ) ​ X t ⊤ , n < m , Q ^ bu , t = Q ^ t − Q ^ sp , t . \widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{sp},t}=\begin{cases}X_{t}(X_{t}^{\top}\widehat{Q}_{t}),&m\leq n,\\ (\widehat{Q}_{t}X_{t})X_{t}^{\top},&n<m,\end{cases}\qquad\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{bu},t}=\widehat{Q}_{t}-\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{sp},t}. (17) These components use the tracked subspace and its orthogonal complement, which can differ from the exact spike and bulk bands. The raw direction is D ~ t = Q ^ sp , t + ρ ​ Q ^ bu , t = ρ ​ Q ^ t − ( ρ − 1 ) ​ Q ^ sp , t . \widetilde{D}_{t}=\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{sp},t}+\rho\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{bu},t}=\rho\widehat{Q}_{t}-(\rho-1)\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{sp},t}. Since X t ​ X t ⊤ X_{t}X_{t}^{\top} is an orthogonal projector, ⟨ Q ^ sp , t , Q ^ bu , t ⟩ F = 0 . \left\langle\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{sp},t},\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{bu},t}\right\rangle_{F}=0. Writing a t = ‖ Q ^ t ‖ F 2 , b t = ‖ Q ^ sp , t ‖ F 2 a_{t}=\|\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F}^{2},\qquad b_{t}=\|\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{sp},t}\|_{F}^{2} therefore gives ‖ Q ^ bu , t ‖ F 2 = a t − b t \|\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{bu},t}\|_{F}^{2}=a_{t}-b_{t} . For nonzero Q ^ t \widehat{Q}_{t} and D ~ t \widetilde{D}_{t} , ‖ D ~ t ‖ F 2 = b t + ρ 2 ​ ( a t − b t ) , c ^ ρ , t = a t b t + ρ 2 ​ ( a t − b t ) = ‖ Q ^ t ‖ F ‖ D ~ t ‖ F . \|\widetilde{D}_{t}\|_{F}^{2}=b_{t}+\rho^{2}(a_{t}-b_{t}),\qquad\widehat{c}_{\rho,t}=\sqrt{\frac{a_{t}}{b_{t}+\rho^{2}(a_{t}-b_{t})}}=\frac{\|\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F}}{\|\widetilde{D}_{t}\|_{F}}. (18) Thus D ^ t = c ^ ρ , t ​ D ~ t \widehat{D}_{t}=\widehat{c}_{\rho,t}\widetilde{D}_{t} satisfies ‖ D ^ t ‖ F = ‖ Q ^ t ‖ F \|\widehat{D}_{t}\|_{F}=\|\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F} . The projected norm can be evaluated on the smaller side: b t = { ‖ X t ⊤ ​ Q ^ t ‖ F 2 , m ≤ n , ‖ Q ^ t ​ X t ‖ F 2 , n < m . b_{t}=\begin{cases}\|X_{t}^{\top}\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F}^{2},&m\leq n,\\ \|\widehat{Q}_{t}X_{t}\|_{F}^{2},&n<m.\end{cases} For a t > 0 a_{t}>0 and ρ > 0 \rho>0 , the raw norm is positive because 0 ≤ b t ≤ a t 0\leq b_{t}\leq a_{t} . At ρ = 0 \rho=0 , a nonzero projected spike component is required. A zero Q ^ t \widehat{Q}_{t} gives a zero numerical update, without evaluating the norm ratio. At ρ = 1 \rho=1 , D ~ t = Q ^ t \widetilde{D}_{t}=\widehat{Q}_{t} , so the update reduces to the unreweighted numerical polar direction.

sections.heading: Relation to the exact target.
sections.text: If Q ^ t = Q t \widehat{Q}_{t}=Q_{t} and M t M_{t} has full rank, then Q t ​ Q t ⊤ = I m when ​ m ≤ n , Q t ⊤ ​ Q t = I n when ​ n < m . Q_{t}Q_{t}^{\top}=I_{m}\quad\text{when }m\leq n,\qquad Q_{t}^{\top}Q_{t}=I_{n}\quad\text{when }n<m. Consequently, a t = d a_{t}=d and b t = r ^ t b_{t}=\widehat{r}_{t} for any orthonormal tracked basis, giving c ^ ρ , t = c ρ , r ^ t \widehat{c}_{\rho,t}=c_{\rho,\widehat{r}_{t}} whenever the raw direction is nonzero. This equality of normalizers does not require an exact spike subspace. If X t X_{t} also spans the selected spike subspace, then r ^ t = r t \widehat{r}_{t}=r_{t} and the numerical construction recovers the exact target D t ​ ( w t ( ρ ) ) D_{t}(w_{t}^{(\rho)}) . For an approximate polar factor, a t a_{t} need not equal d d and b t b_{t} need not equal r ^ t \widehat{r}_{t} , so the normalizers can differ. For rank-deficient inputs, the direct norm ratio remains applicable, but the full-rank simplification above does not apply in general.

sections.heading: Finite-precision computation.
sections.text: The direct norm ratio in equation 12 requires only Frobenius norms and rescaling. Its norm-matching property does not rely on exact orthogonality of the computed components, unlike the expression involving a t − b t a_{t}-b_{t} . For a nonzero computed raw direction, exact evaluation of the ratio matches its norm to ‖ Q ^ t ‖ F \|\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F} ; finite-precision evaluation is subject to rounding error. Norm matching controls magnitude without correcting polar or subspace approximation errors.

sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details and SVD-Free Algorithm
sections.text: This appendix gives the implementation details behind Section 3 . It covers noise calibration, the exact-SVD target used in oracle comparisons, spike tracking for both variants, and the full BB-Adaptive algorithm. BB-Static and BB-Adaptive share the reweighting and normalization of Section 2 . They differ only in how they choose and track the spike band. Appendix B.4 derives numerical norm matching, and Proposition 4 derives the half-batch noise estimate and the Nesterov noise factor.

sections.heading: Half-batch noise estimate.
sections.text: The two halves in equation 5 are sampled independently at the same parameters, so they have the same mean. This mean cancels in the half-batch difference Z t split Z_{t}^{\mathrm{split}} . After vectorization, Z t split Z_{t}^{\mathrm{split}} has the same covariance as the sampling noise in G t raw G_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}} . Hence s ^ t 2 = ‖ Z t split ‖ F 2 / ( m ​ n ) \widehat{s}_{t}^{\,2}=\|Z_{t}^{\mathrm{split}}\|_{F}^{2}/(mn) estimates the average entrywise noise variance of the full-minibatch gradient. For isotropic noise, this is the common entrywise variance. For anisotropic noise, one scalar cannot describe the full covariance.

sections.heading: Clipping and variance smoothing.
sections.text: Let χ t ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \chi_{t}\in(0,1] be the global clipping scalar. It is computed from the raw full-minibatch gradient of all model parameters, and all matrices share it. Each matrix uses G t = χ t ​ G t raw G_{t}=\chi_{t}G_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}} in the momentum recursion. The halves are not clipped separately. Instead, each matrix’s raw variance estimate is scaled by χ t 2 \chi_{t}^{2} before smoothing: s ¯ t 2 = { χ t 2 ​ s ^ t 2 , if the variance state is uninitialized , γ ​ s ¯ t − 1 2 + ( 1 − γ ) ​ χ t 2 ​ s ^ t 2 , otherwise . \overline{s}_{t}^{\,2}=\begin{cases}\chi_{t}^{2}\widehat{s}_{t}^{\,2},&\text{if the variance state is uninitialized},\\[2.0pt] \gamma\overline{s}_{t-1}^{\,2}+(1-\gamma)\chi_{t}^{2}\widehat{s}_{t}^{\,2},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The EMA averages variances. The square root s ¯ t 2 \sqrt{\overline{s}_{t}^{\,2}} in equation 8 is taken afterwards. For a matrix first observed at step 1 1 , this gives s ¯ 1 2 = χ 1 2 ​ s ^ 1 2 \overline{s}_{1}^{\,2}=\chi_{1}^{2}\widehat{s}_{1}^{\,2} . Without clipping, χ t = 1 \chi_{t}=1 .

sections.heading: Nesterov factor.
sections.text: Proposition 4 derives the factor ν t ​ ( β ) \nu_{t}(\beta) in equation 7 under a reference model: centered, isotropic noise that is independent over time and has constant variance, with B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Writing M t = ( 1 − β 2 ) ​ G t + β 2 ​ B t − 1 M_{t}=(1-\beta^{2})G_{t}+\beta^{2}B_{t-1} gives an equivalent two-term form: ν t 2 ​ ( β ) = ( 1 − β 2 ) 2 + β 4 ​ 1 − β 1 + β ​ ( 1 − β 2 ​ ( t − 1 ) ) . \nu_{t}^{2}(\beta)=(1-\beta^{2})^{2}+\beta^{4}\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}\left(1-\beta^{2(t-1)}\right). The first term comes from the current gradient, which enters M t M_{t} both directly and through the updated buffer. The second term comes from the past gradients stored in B t − 1 B_{t-1} .

sections.heading: Approximations.
sections.text: The implementation replaces the reference variance with the clipping-scaled running estimate s ¯ t 2 \overline{s}_{t}^{\,2} . This puts the estimate on the scale of the applied gradient. Because χ t \chi_{t} depends on the data, the scaled estimate is in general biased for the noise in the clipped gradient. The running estimate also assumes that the noise level changes slowly. Finally, the noise edge assumes Gaussian white noise (Section 2 ). The multiplier κ edge \kappa_{\mathrm{edge}} can shift the threshold, but a single scalar cannot correct for anisotropic or correlated noise in general. The experiments use γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 and κ edge = 1 \kappa_{\mathrm{edge}}=1 .

sections.heading: C.2 Exact Target and Oracle Comparison
sections.text: For a full-rank input M t M_{t} and a nonzero two-level profile, the exact-SVD oracle evaluates, for either rule, D t svd = D t ​ ( w t ( ρ ) ) = c ρ , r t ​ U t ​ diag ⁡ ( w t ( ρ ) ) ​ V t ⊤ . D_{t}^{\mathrm{svd}}=D_{t}\!\left(w_{t}^{(\rho)}\right)=c_{\rho,r_{t}}U_{t}\operatorname{diag}\!\left(w_{t}^{(\rho)}\right)V_{t}^{\top}. (19) For BB-Adaptive , r t r_{t} counts all singular values above the threshold τ t = τ ^ t \tau_{t}=\widehat{\tau}_{t} . For BB-Static , r t = ⌈ p ​ d ⌉ r_{t}=\lceil pd\rceil . In both cases, c ρ , r t c_{\rho,r_{t}} is the normalizer in equation 4 . Rank-deficient and zero inputs follow Appendix B.3 . Here, oracle only means that the rule is evaluated exactly with an SVD. It does not choose the partition or the gain. An oracle comparison fixes M t M_{t} , the rule, and ρ \rho . Both realizations therefore use the same threshold for BB-Adaptive and the same rank for BB-Static . The exact oracle matches ‖ Q t ‖ F \|Q_{t}\|_{F} , and the numerical realization matches ‖ Q ^ t ‖ F \|\widehat{Q}_{t}\|_{F} . If Q ^ t = Q t \widehat{Q}_{t}=Q_{t} and the orthonormal tracked basis spans the selected spike subspace, the numerical update equals the oracle (Appendix B.4 ). For BB-Adaptive , the rank cap applies only to the numerical tracker. The exact target keeps every direction above the threshold. Both sides use the same spectral rule, so a comparison at a common input measures only numerical error: polar approximation, imperfect subspace recovery, and, for BB-Adaptive , truncation by the cap.

sections.heading: C.3 Warm-Started Block Iteration
sections.text: This subsection first gives the tracker for BB-Adaptive and then the simpler tracker for BB-Static . Both use the smaller-side Gram operator K t ∈ ℝ d × d K_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} from equation 10 . Its action on a block Y Y is K t ​ Y = { M t ​ ( M t ⊤ ​ Y ) , m ≤ n , M t ⊤ ​ ( M t ​ Y ) , n < m , K_{t}Y=\begin{cases}M_{t}(M_{t}^{\top}Y),&m\leq n,\\ M_{t}^{\top}(M_{t}Y),&n<m,\end{cases} so the Gram matrix is never formed. As in Section 3.2 , orth \operatorname{orth} returns an orthonormal basis of the column space of its argument. An empty column space gives an empty basis.

sections.heading: Initialization and trial-space construction.
sections.text: Let X t − 1 X_{t-1} be the spike basis that BB-Adaptive retained at the previous step, with r ^ t − 1 \widehat{r}_{t-1} columns. Before the first update, X 0 X_{0} is empty and r ^ 0 = 0 \widehat{r}_{0}=0 . For positive initial and refresh probe widths n init n_{\mathrm{init}} and n probe n_{\mathrm{probe}} , set n fresh , t = { min ⁡ { d , n init } , r ^ t − 1 = 0 , min ⁡ { d , n probe } , r ^ t − 1 > 0 . n_{\mathrm{fresh},t}=\begin{cases}\min\{d,n_{\mathrm{init}}\},&\widehat{r}_{t-1}=0,\\ \min\{d,n_{\mathrm{probe}}\},&\widehat{r}_{t-1}>0.\end{cases} The initial width is also used whenever the previous step selected no directions. Draw Ω t ∈ ℝ d × n fresh , t \Omega_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n_{\mathrm{fresh},t}} with independent standard Gaussian entries and set Y 0 = orth ⁡ ( [ X t − 1 , Ω t ] ) . Y_{0}=\operatorname{orth}([X_{t-1},\Omega_{t}]). The concatenated block may have more than d d columns, but its orthonormal basis has at most d d . The previous basis gives a warm start, and the fresh probes let new directions enter the trial space. At the first step, Y 0 Y_{0} comes from the probes alone. The first retained basis X 1 X_{1} is obtained only after iteration and threshold selection.

sections.heading: Block iteration and Ritz extraction.
sections.text: Within training step t t , perform q q block-power iterations: Y j + 1 = orth ( K t Y j ) , j = 0 , … , q − 1 . Y_{j+1}=\operatorname{orth}(K_{t}Y_{j}),\qquad j=0,\ldots,q-1. (20) Let ℓ t \ell_{t} be the number of columns of Y q Y_{q} . For a nonempty trial basis, form T t = Y q ⊤ ​ K t ​ Y q = O t ​ Λ t ​ O t ⊤ , λ t , 1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ λ t , ℓ t ≥ 0 , T_{t}=Y_{q}^{\top}K_{t}Y_{q}=O_{t}\Lambda_{t}O_{t}^{\top},\qquad\lambda_{t,1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{t,\ell_{t}}\geq 0, where Λ t = diag ⁡ ( λ t , 1 , … , λ t , ℓ t ) \Lambda_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{t,1},\ldots,\lambda_{t,\ell_{t}}) . The Ritz directions are the columns of Y q ​ O t Y_{q}O_{t} , with singular-value estimates λ t , i \sqrt{\lambda_{t,i}} . The eigenvalues are nonnegative in exact arithmetic because K t K_{t} is positive semidefinite. For a nonnegative integer rank cap r max r_{\max} , let n cand , t n_{\mathrm{cand},t} count the Ritz values above the threshold: n cand , t = | { i ∈ [ ℓ t ] : λ t , i > τ ^ t 2 } | , r ^ t = min ⁡ { n cand , t , r max } , X t = orth ⁡ ( Y q ​ O t , [ r ^ t ] ) . n_{\mathrm{cand},t}=\bigl|\{i\in[\ell_{t}]:\lambda_{t,i}>\widehat{\tau}_{t}^{\,2}\}\bigr|,\qquad\widehat{r}_{t}=\min\{n_{\mathrm{cand},t},r_{\max}\},\qquad X_{t}=\operatorname{orth}\!\left(Y_{q}O_{t,[\widehat{r}_{t}]}\right). (21) Here O t , [ r ^ t ] O_{t,[\widehat{r}_{t}]} holds the first r ^ t \widehat{r}_{t} eigenvectors in decreasing eigenvalue order. If the cap binds, the largest estimates above the threshold are kept. An empty selection gives an empty spike basis. If ℓ t = 0 \ell_{t}=0 , set r ^ t = 0 \widehat{r}_{t}=0 and leave X t X_{t} empty; no eigendecomposition is needed. The experiments use this hard threshold without hysteresis. The selected Ritz block is reorthonormalized before it is stored. The projector identities in Appendix B.4 assume orthonormal columns, so in finite precision they hold only up to orthonormalization error.

sections.heading: Experimental settings and random-number state.
sections.text: All BB-Adaptive training runs use q = 6 , n init = 128 , n probe = 128 , r max = 256 . q=6,\qquad n_{\mathrm{init}}=128,\qquad n_{\mathrm{probe}}=128,\qquad r_{\max}=256. Probe widths are limited by d d . The cap r max r_{\max} is an absolute number of directions and does not scale with d d . The retained rank satisfies r ^ t ≤ min ⁡ { ℓ t , r max } \widehat{r}_{t}\leq\min\{\ell_{t},r_{\max}\} , with ℓ t ≤ d \ell_{t}\leq d . The first retained basis has at most min ⁡ { d , 128 } \min\{d,128\} columns, below the cap. The cap applies only to the retained basis. In these runs, the trial space has up to min ⁡ { d , r ^ t − 1 + 128 } \min\{d,\widehat{r}_{t-1}+128\} columns, which can exceed the cap. Gaussian probes are generated in float32 with a dedicated pseudorandom-number generator for each parameter matrix, separate from the training random-number stream. Its state carries over from step to step and is never reseeded.

sections.heading: Fixed-rank tracking ( BB-Static ).
sections.text: BB-Static tracks a block of fixed width r = ⌈ p ​ d ⌉ r=\lceil pd\rceil . The fraction p p is shared across matrices and fixed for the whole run. If a stored basis X t − 1 ∈ ℝ d × r X_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} exists, it is the warm start, Y 0 = X t − 1 Y_{0}=X_{t-1} . Otherwise, as at the first step, we draw a Gaussian block Ω t ∈ ℝ d × r \Omega_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} and set Y 0 = orth ⁡ ( Ω t ) Y_{0}=\operatorname{orth}(\Omega_{t}) . At each training step, we run Y j + 1 = orth ( K t Y j ) , j = 0 , … , q − 1 , X t = Y q , Y_{j+1}=\operatorname{orth}(K_{t}Y_{j}),\qquad j=0,\ldots,q-1,\qquad X_{t}=Y_{q}, with q = 6 q=6 in the experiments. The whole final basis enters equation 11 and is stored for the next step. Unlike the BB-Adaptive tracker, this tracker adds no fresh probes, does no Ritz extraction, and applies no threshold or rank cap. The parameters n init n_{\mathrm{init}} , n probe n_{\mathrm{probe}} , and r max r_{\max} therefore do not apply. For example, p = 0.20 p=0.20 and d = 1024 d=1024 give r = 205 r=205 , so initialization and all six iterations use a 1024 × 205 1024\times 205 block.

sections.heading: C.4 Full Algorithm
sections.text: Algorithm 1 gives one BB-Adaptive step for one matrix. It combines noise calibration, spike tracking, and numerical norm matching. It returns the update direction before learning-rate scaling. The clipping scalar χ t \chi_{t} is computed once from the full-model gradient and passed in. For BB-Static , the noise-estimate and threshold steps are skipped, and the fixed-rank tracker of Appendix C.3 replaces the adaptive one. Before the first update, B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , X 0 X_{0} is empty, and the variance state is uninitialized. The algorithm returns B t B_{t} , X t X_{t} , and s ¯ t 2 \overline{s}_{t}^{\,2} along with D ^ t \widehat{D}_{t} . The probe generator’s state is kept separately for each matrix. sections.heading: Appendix D Band Content Along Muon Trajectories
sections.text: Does the bulk, whose singular values lie at or below the noise edge, contribute meaningfully to reference-gradient alignment under the flat profile? We examine this question along Muon trajectories of continued pretraining, measuring band sizes, per-direction alignment, and signed contributions across matrices. The measured bulk is weak per direction but substantial in aggregate : it contains 93.7–97.1% of pooled singular directions and has positive signed aggregate alignment in every analyzed matrix. These observations motivate a broad-bulk/small-spike partition and the fixed fractions tested in Section 5 . Whether increasing the bulk’s relative gain improves an update is a separate question, which Appendix E examines.

sections.heading: Training trajectories and checkpoints.
sections.text: For each of FineMath-4, CodeParrot, and Wiki-ar, we analyze one Pythia-70M Muon trajectory of continued pretraining. Each run uses approximately 100M tokens, with batches of 32 sequences of length 1024, momentum β = 0.95 \beta=0.95 , global gradient clipping at norm 1, and Newton–Schulz iterations for the polar map, as in the Muon baseline of Section 5 . The matrix optimizer and the auxiliary AdamW optimizer both use peak learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , the shared Pythia-70M rate of Section 5 . These diagnostics observe the Muon trajectories without changing their updates. We report four checkpoints as 0.0M, 25.0M, 50.0M, and 99.9M consumed training tokens. The initial measurement is a transient probe before continued pretraining; subsequent measurements precede updates after 24,969,216, 49,971,200, and 99,942,400 tokens. At each checkpoint, we analyze all 24 hidden weight matrices, excluding embeddings and the language-model head. For matrix ℓ \ell with dimensions m ℓ × n ℓ m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell} , write d ℓ = min ⁡ { m ℓ , n ℓ } d_{\ell}=\min\{m_{\ell},n_{\ell}\} . Here each matrix supplies 512 thin-SVD directions, giving N dir = ∑ ℓ d ℓ = 12,288 N_{\mathrm{dir}}=\sum_{\ell}d_{\ell}=12{,}288 directions per corpus–checkpoint–frame combination.

sections.heading: Positive alignment is present in every measured matrix.
sections.text: All 24 matrices have positive signed bulk sums at every checkpoint in both frames and all three corpora: 3 × 4 × 2 × 24 = 576 3\times 4\times 2\times 24=576 recorded combinations. Positive bulk alignment is therefore spread across all layers.

sections.heading: The optimizer’s frame changes the relative contributions.
sections.text: At 99.9M tokens, the Nesterov bulk supplies 63.5% of pooled signed alignment on FineMath-4, 45.8% on CodeParrot, and 25.3% on Wiki-ar. The paired raw-gradient shares are 18.6%, 16.6%, and 18.1%. A larger share does not necessarily mean a larger absolute bulk contribution: in Table 5 , the final Nesterov bulk sums are smaller than their raw-gradient counterparts, but the spike sums decrease by a greater proportion. The share is also not monotone over training: on FineMath-4, the Nesterov bulk share is 24.7% at 25M, 10.0% at 50M, and 63.5% at 99.9M. What holds in every case is positive net bulk alignment; the share itself varies across corpora and checkpoints.

sections.heading: Motivation for the fixed-fraction sweep.
sections.text: The complementary spike band contains only 2.9–6.3% of the pooled singular directions in these measurements. This broad-bulk/small-spike structure motivates testing small fixed spike fractions, alongside larger ones, in Table 9 (Appendix G.2 ). The tested grid is p ∈ { 0.015 , 0.02 , 0.05 , 0.15 , 0.20 } p\in\{0.015,0.02,0.05,0.15,0.20\} : 5% lies within the observed pooled range and is the default for BB-Static , 1.5% and 2% examine smaller fractions, and 15% and 20% examine larger spike bands. The diagnostics inform the grid; we did not convert the noise edge into five calibrated fractions. The loss comparisons in Table 9 decide which fractions perform best. The 2.9–6.3% range is computed after pooling matrices within each corpus–checkpoint–frame combination. Individual matrices can fall outside it, and it is not an estimate of the best fixed rank. BB-Static uses r t , ℓ = ⌈ p ​ d ℓ ⌉ r_{t,\ell}=\lceil pd_{\ell}\rceil with a fixed fraction for the whole run, whereas BB-Adaptive selects the spike band separately for each matrix and step. The two rules give different partitions even when their pooled band sizes are similar.

sections.heading: Link to the two-band design.
sections.text: Theorem 2 shows that a shared bulk gain needs only the polar factor plus a correction in the spike subspace. The band-content measurements show why the bulk matters in this allocation: it carries positive reference alignment in every matrix. Appendix E.2 evaluates the post-update effect of reweighting, and Section 5 evaluates training performance and computational cost.

sections.heading: Appendix E Pre-Update Alignment and Post-Update Loss
sections.text: This appendix connects the band-content measurements in Appendix D to the effect of spectral reweighting on validation loss. We first compute the pre-update reference-alignment preference and then evaluate the model produced by a controlled update. The single-update measurements show that finite bulk-emphasizing reweighting can improve on the exact flat update Q t Q_{t} , even when paired pre-update predictions favor less bulk weight.

sections.heading: Interpreting the norm-matched reweighting.
sections.text: Increasing ρ \rho moves the fixed direction norm from the spikes toward the bulk. For a matrix with 95% bulk directions, the applied bulk gains at ρ = 2 \rho=2 and 4 4 are approximately 1.019 1.019 and 1.024 1.024 , whereas the spike gains are 0.510 0.510 and 0.256 0.256 . In the pre-update score, the loss of spike alignment outweighs the additional bulk alignment, which explains the preference for smaller ρ \rho . Relative bulk emphasis and relative spike suppression therefore describe the same norm-matched intervention. The next subsection evaluates its effect directly on post-update validation loss.

sections.heading: Question and controlled comparison.
sections.text: Can a finite increase in the bulk-to-spike gain lower validation loss after one update, even when a pre-update linearized prediction favors less bulk weight? We use the Pythia-70M Muon trajectories of Appendix D on FineMath-4, CodeParrot, and Wiki-ar, immediately before updates 763 and 1526, after 24,969,216 and 49,971,200 training tokens, respectively. The protocol uses batches of 32 sequences of length 1024, β = 0.95 \beta=0.95 , γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 , κ edge = 1 \kappa_{\mathrm{edge}}=1 , global clipping at norm 1, and peak learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for both the matrix and auxiliary optimizers. Validation uses 128 fixed held-out windows. At each checkpoint, the branches share the current Nesterov singular frames and the noise-edge partitions of Appendix D . We vary one common gain across the 24 hidden weight matrices, using the exact-SVD target and separate Frobenius norm matching for each matrix. The tested gains are ρ ∈ { 0.5 , 0.75 , 1 , 1.25 , 1.5 } \rho\in\{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5\} , with two duplicate ρ = 1 \rho=1 branches. The comparator is the exact flat update Q t Q_{t} at the same input, computed from the same SVD. All branches compute their current update from the same exact SVD, so they differ only in ρ \rho . We report K = 0 K=0 : validation immediately after the current update, without additional training steps. The duplicate ρ = 1 \rho=1 branches have identical recorded losses.

sections.heading: Bulk emphasis improves the post-update model.
sections.text: Both ρ = 1.25 \rho=1.25 and ρ = 1.5 \rho=1.5 lower validation loss relative to ρ = 1 \rho=1 in five of six corpus–checkpoint settings: all three corpora at 25M tokens, and CodeParrot and Wiki-ar at 50M tokens. The positive loss reductions B ^ ϵ \widehat{B}_{\epsilon} measure these improvements directly. FineMath-4 at 50M is the exception, where the flat update has lower loss than both bulk-emphasizing updates. The improvements occur despite paired pre-update linearized predictions favoring less bulk weight at both perturbation widths in every tested state. These predictions are recorded for the intervention branches and differ from the pooled score J ⁡ ( ρ ) J(\rho) in Appendix E.1 . Thus, finite, norm-matched spectral reweighting can improve the post-update model even when the paired pre-update approximation favors the opposite allocation. The benefit is already visible at K = 0 K=0 , without additional continuation steps.

sections.heading: Continuation utility evaluates the updated model.
sections.text: Even at K = 0 K=0 , the evaluation point has changed. For an additive intervention with fixed effective step multiplier η t , ℓ \eta_{t,\ell} , let θ 1 + \theta_{1}^{+} be the complete parameter state after the flat update, and let ℰ \mathcal{E} be the evaluation objective defining the loss. Differentiation with respect to an applied singular-direction gain gives u ℓ , i , t , 0 = η t , ℓ ​ ⟨ ∇ W ℓ ℰ ​ ( θ 1 + ) , u t , ℓ , i ​ v t , ℓ , i ⊤ ⟩ F . u_{\ell,i,t,0}=\eta_{t,\ell}\left\langle\nabla_{W_{\ell}}\mathcal{E}(\theta_{1}^{+}),u_{t,\ell,i}v_{t,\ell,i}^{\top}\right\rangle_{F}. (39) The singular vectors remain those of the fixed pre-intervention Nesterov input, but the evaluation gradient is taken after the flat update. The chain rule uses ∂ W ℓ + ∂ w ℓ , i = − η t , ℓ ​ u t , ℓ , i ​ v t , ℓ , i ⊤ , \frac{\partial W_{\ell}^{+}}{\partial w_{\ell,i}}=-\eta_{t,\ell}u_{t,\ell,i}v_{t,\ell,i}^{\top}, and continuation utility is the negative loss derivative. The multiplier η t , ℓ \eta_{t,\ell} includes the learning rate and fixed shape scaling. Thus, “first order” describes changes in the applied gains around the flat update, with the actual parameter-update step size held fixed. This identifies the evaluation point relevant to local allocation preferences and explains the difference from pre-update reference alignment.

sections.heading: What the experiment establishes.
sections.text: The experiment provides direct evidence that finite, norm-matched two-band reweighting can improve the model produced by a single update, already at K = 0 K=0 . The measurements cover ρ = 1.25 \rho=1.25 and 1.5 1.5 at checkpoints near 25M and 50M tokens; Appendix D also measures band content at initialization and 99.9M. Section 5 separately evaluates the full training rule with the shared default ρ = 4 \rho=4 . Because norm matching couples relative bulk emphasis with spike suppression, the measured benefit concerns their combined reweighting.

sections.heading: What finer shaping can add.
sections.text: Two bands can use u bt u_{\mathrm{bt}} , the differences between band means. They cannot use u wi u_{\mathrm{wi}} , the variation within bands. By Step 1, every differentiable curve of norm-matched gains through 𝟏 d \mathbf{1}_{d} , however fine-grained, has its velocity in 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . By Step 3, its first-order rate per unit velocity is therefore at most ‖ u ⟂ ‖ 2 \|u_{\perp}\|_{2} . The best two-band change reaches ‖ u bt ‖ 2 \|u_{\mathrm{bt}}\|_{2} . Finer shaping can thus add at most ‖ u ⟂ ‖ 2 − ‖ u bt ‖ 2 = ( 1 − R bt ) ​ ‖ u ⟂ ‖ 2 ≤ ‖ u wi ‖ 2 \|u_{\perp}\|_{2}-\|u_{\mathrm{bt}}\|_{2}=(1-R_{\mathrm{bt}})\|u_{\perp}\|_{2}\leq\|u_{\mathrm{wi}}\|_{2} to the first-order rate. In particular, if utilities are constant within each band, finer shaping cannot improve on two bands to first order. The discussion after Theorem 1 covers the remaining caveats.

sections.heading: Models and datasets.
sections.text: We conduct continued pretraining by adapting converged , publicly available Pythia checkpoints on new corpora with the cross-entropy loss. We use five scales, Pythia-14M, 31M, 70M, 160M, and 410M, with hidden widths d model = 128 d_{\mathrm{model}}=128 , 256, 512, 768, and 1024, respectively. For the matrix methods, AdamW updates the embeddings and the language-model head. Table 15 in Appendix G lists the widths, batch settings, and training budgets. Pythia was pretrained on the Pile ( Gao et al., 2021 ) , a mainly English mixture that includes GitHub code, English Wikipedia, and arXiv. We adapt it to six corpora in three groups. For mathematics, FineMath-4 and FineMath-3 ( Allal et al., 2025 ) come from Common Crawl with different math-quality thresholds. For code, CodeParrot is CodeParrot-clean ( CodeParrot, 2022 ) , a filtered and deduplicated Python corpus from GitHub. For multilingual text, Wiki-de, Wiki-zh, and Wiki-ar are German, Chinese, and Arabic Wikipedia.

sections.heading: Initial loss reflects corpus shift.
sections.text: Table 8 reports the pre-adaptation held-out loss ℓ 0 \ell_{0} and the change Δ = ℓ final − ℓ 0 \Delta=\ell_{\mathrm{final}}-\ell_{0} after 100M tokens of continued pretraining with Muon . We use ℓ 0 \ell_{0} as a proxy for how far each corpus is from the Pythia pretraining distribution. A lower ℓ 0 \ell_{0} means that the pretrained model already assigns higher probability to the corpus. A higher ℓ 0 \ell_{0} suggests a larger distribution shift. The corpora keep the same order at every scale. CodeParrot has the lowest ℓ 0 \ell_{0} , as GitHub code is already part of the Pile. Wiki-de and Wiki-zh have the highest ℓ 0 \ell_{0} , as they are far from the mainly English Pile. The two math corpora, which overlap with mathematical text in the Pile, lie in between. Wiki-ar also lies in between, below FineMath-4 and above FineMath-3 at every scale. Continued pretraining with Muon lowers the validation loss in every setting, but a larger ℓ 0 \ell_{0} does not always give a larger reduction. For example, Wiki-ar starts below FineMath-4 yet gains about twice as much at every scale. FineMath-4 has higher ℓ 0 \ell_{0} than FineMath-3 and gains more at every scale. CodeParrot starts with the lowest ℓ 0 \ell_{0} and has the smallest reductions at 160M and 410M, with Δ = − 0.479 \Delta=-0.479 at 14M and − 0.118 -0.118 at 410M. Among the multilingual corpora, Wiki-de starts with the highest ℓ 0 \ell_{0} . Wiki-zh and Wiki-ar keep large gains through 160M and still improve by about 0.7 0.7 at 410M. Thus, ℓ 0 \ell_{0} describes how well the pretrained model already fits a corpus, while Δ \Delta records the change achieved within the adaptation budget.

sections.heading: Fixed fraction versus noise calibration.
sections.text: Both variants use the same norm-matched two-level rule with ρ = 4 \rho=4 . They differ in how they choose the split and in how they track the spike subspace (Appendix C.3 ). Table 9 shows that the best fixed fraction varies across models and corpora. BB-Adaptive instead sets the split for each matrix and step from the noise edge. On average, it keeps 4.6 % 4.6\% of d model d_{\mathrm{model}} directions as spikes (5th–95th percentile: 1.3 1.3 – 7.7 % 7.7\% ; per-corpus means: 2.8 2.8 – 5.8 % 5.8\% ). Without any fraction search, it performs on par with the shared BB-Static (5%) . Their aggregate losses are close (Table 2 ), and BB-Adaptive has lower loss in 10 settings, higher loss in 6, and equal loss in 14. BB-Static (5%) has the lower per-step cost (Table 14 ). Selecting the fraction for each setting gives further gains: BB-Static † has lower loss than BB-Adaptive in 20 settings, higher loss in 4, and equal loss in 6 (Table 1 ). Noise calibration thus removes the fraction search, a shared fraction lowers the per-step cost, and per-setting selection lowers the loss further at an extra tuning cost.

sections.heading: Adding a third band.
sections.text: We also test whether a finer split improves on two bands. The three-band variant of BB-Static splits the singular directions of each matrix into the leading 5%, the next 15%, and the remaining 80%. Its leading band is the same as in BB-Static (5%) , so the comparison isolates the effect of splitting the bulk into two parts. Averaged over all 30 30 model–corpus settings, the three-band variant ends with a final loss 0.002 ± 0.001 0.002\pm 0.001 higher than BB-Static (5%) . The extra band therefore does not help, and two bands remain the better choice. This is consistent with Theorem 1 , under which a finer split can improve on two bands only through utility differences within the bands.

sections.heading: Single-update allocation experiment.
sections.text: On Pythia-70M Muon trajectories for FineMath-4, CodeParrot, and Wiki-ar, we compare exact-SVD updates with ρ = 1.25 \rho=1.25 and 1.5 1.5 against the exact flat update ρ = 1 \rho=1 near 25M and 50M tokens. Each comparison fixes the current singular frames and noise-edge partitions, applies a common ρ \rho across 24 hidden weight matrices, and matches each matrix’s Frobenius direction norm separately. Both bulk-emphasizing gains lower the validation loss immediately after the update in five of six corpus–checkpoint settings, despite paired pre-update linearized predictions that favor less bulk weight. These K = 0 K=0 measurements illustrate the difference between pre-update alignment and the post-update loss response studied in Theorem 1 . Appendix E.2 gives the protocol, and Table 7 reports all six settings.

sections.heading: Gain sensitivity and numerical accuracy.
sections.text: For BB-Adaptive , we sweep ρ ∈ { 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 } \rho\in\{2,4,6,8,10\} across 30 model–corpus settings using 20M tokens, one seed, and the shared learning rates (Table 12 ). Within a setting, the loss changes by a median of 0.009 0.009 across the tested gains, with larger changes at 70M. The best tested gain improves on ρ = 4 \rho=4 by about 0.0045 0.0045 on average. The smallest gain, ρ = 2 \rho=2 , is best in 20 settings. We keep ρ = 4 \rho=4 as the shared default in all 100M-token runs. The sweep covers bulk-emphasizing gains, and Appendix E.2 studies gains near ρ = 1 \rho=1 . At ρ = 4 \rho=4 , the per-scale median effective gains ρ eff \rho_{\mathrm{eff}} lie in [ 3.963 , 4.005 ] [3.963,4.005] , and the per-scale median Rayleigh–Ritz residuals stay below 10 − 5 10^{-5} (Table 13 ). These diagnostics check the realized gain and the accuracy of the retained spike subspaces. sections.heading: Effect of the spike fraction in BB-Static .
sections.text: Table 9 presents the results of tuning the fixed fraction p p used by BB-Static . The optimal value varies substantially across model scales and corpora. Thus, no single value of p p is optimal across all experiments, and selecting one requires an expensive tuning of parameter p p . In contrast, BB-Adaptive determines the rank directly from the spectrum of each matrix using the Marchenko–Pastur noise edge. It selects, on average, 4.6 % 4.6\% of d model d_{\mathrm{model}} (5th–95th percentile: 1.3 % 1.3\% – 7.7 % 7.7\% ; per-corpus means: 2.8 % 2.8\% – 5.8 % 5.8\% ) and, without tuning, closely matches the best fixed fraction across scales. The shared p = 5 % p=5\% configuration achieves aggregate validation loss comparable to BB-Adaptive (Table 2 ). Table 1 instead reports BB-Static † , selected separately for each model–corpus setting from the five fractions in Table 9 . The benefit of the adaptive rule is therefore not improved accuracy over a tuned fixed fraction, but achieving comparable accuracy without the tuning .
