Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.07497v1 [cs.AI] 05 Oct 2026 Does Muon Need Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping? Meher Chaitanya Tianyi Zhou & Aristides Gionis Affiliation: KTH Royal Institute of Technology Affiliation: Stockholm, Sweden Email: {mcpi,tzho,argioni}@kth.se Abstract Muon combines current and past gradients into matrix momentum. For M = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ M=U\Sigma V^{	op} , the idealized polar update Q = U ​ V ⊤ Q=UV^{	op} gives every singular direction the same weight. We refer to this as the flat profile. Several recent optimizers replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that give each direction its own gain. We ask how much of this spectral detail a Muon update needs . Our spectral diagnostics show that approximately 94 94 – 97 % 97\% of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with a reference gradient. We introduce BulkBoost , a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants. The latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko–Pastur reference edge for Muon ’s Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from the spikes above it. Both variants increase the bulk’s relative weight through one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix’s unreweighted direction. For a fixed partition, our theory gives the first-order condition under which moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss. It also quantifies the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate, over all per-mode reallocations, that two bands can capture. A polar-plus-low-rank representation enables an approximation without a full SVD, tracking only the spike subspace. Across 30 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia- 14 14 M to 410 410 M and six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with the fine-grained power-law profile of Freon ( Shumaylov et al., 2026 ) and outperforms Spectra ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Measured against Muon ’s flat profile, Freon reduces final loss by 0.022 % 0.022\% of the pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of 0.073 0.073 – 0.147 % 0.147\% . These observations suggest that useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles. 1 Introduction An optimizer for neural-network weight matrices decides two things: how large an update is, and how the update is spread across directions. Muon , an optimizer for language-model training, combines current and past gradients into a matrix momentum M M ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its SVD, M = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ M=U\Sigma V^{	op} , writes M M as a sum of orthogonal directions weighted by their singular values. The idealized polar update Q = U ​ V ⊤ Q=UV^{	op} keeps these directions but sets every singular value to one . Each direction therefore receives the same gain. We refer to this as the flat profile . Recent optimizers depart from this flat profile through spectral maps U ​ g ​ ( Σ ) ​ V ⊤ Ug(\Sigma)V^{	op} , where the gain varies across singular directions ( Shumaylov et al., 2026 ; Dong & Sawin, 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Pang et al., 2026 ; Feoktistov et al., 2026 ) . At the same time, Shumaylov et al. (2026) show that substantially different spectra, including random and inverted ones, can remain effective. These results raise a more basic question than which detailed profile is best: does Muon need fine-grained spectral shaping, or is a coarse reallocation between two groups of directions enough? Two observations motivate this question. First, a direction’s strength in the sampled momentum, its separation from sampling noise, and the benefit of increasing its update weight are distinct quantities. A small singular value can still carry signal, and a large one need not deserve more weight. Second, our diagnostics reveal a broad spectral bulk and a small leading band. Under a Gaussian white-noise reference model, random matrix theory provides an asymptotic upper spectral edge, the noise edge ( Marchenko & Pastur, 1967 ; Baik et al., 2005 ; Benaych-Georges & Nadakuditi, 2012 ) . We call directions above this reference edge spikes and the remaining directions the bulk . On Pythia-70M Muon trajectories, approximately 93.7 93.7 – 97.1 % 97.1\% of pooled singular modes lie in the bulk (Appendix D ). These below-edge singular modes, the bulk , are weak individually, yet their aggregate signed alignment with an independently sampled reference gradient is positive in every analyzed matrix. Thus, the broad spectral bulk makes a non-negligible collective contribution even though its individual directions are weak. These measurements motivate a two-band partition. We introduce BulkBoost , whose exact target reweights Muon ’s polar direction in two bands. The spike and bulk gains are 1 1 and ρ ho before normalization, and the update is then rescaled to keep the Frobenius norm of the unreweighted direction. At the exact-target level, ρ = 1 ho=1 recovers Q Q , while ρ > 1 ho>1 increases the bulk’s relative weight. Once the partition is chosen, the same ρ ho controls reallocation across all spectrally updated matrices. We consider two rules for the split. The fixed-rank rule , BB-Static , takes a prescribed fraction p p of the leading directions, shared across matrices and held fixed within each run. Our shared configuration uses p = 5 % p=5\% , within the pooled spike fraction of 2.9 2.9 – 6.3 % 6.3\% measured in our diagnostics (Appendix D ). We also test smaller and larger fractions. The noise-calibrated rule , BB-Adaptive , estimates the sampling noise from two minibatch halves, propagates it through the momentum, and places the split at the resulting noise edge for each matrix and step. The edge assumes isotropic Gaussian noise. Since the real gradient noise is not isotropic, this split is an approximation. Our contributions are as follows. 1. A two-band reweighting rule. BulkBoost reweights Muon ’s flat update in two bands with one shared gain. The split between the bands comes either from a fixed fraction of directions or from a noise-calibrated edge. An exact polar-plus-low-rank identity lets us avoid a full SVD (Section 3 ). 2. What the two bands capture. For a fixed partition, we characterize to first order when shifting weight toward the bulk lowers the loss, and how much of the best per-direction improvement two bands can reach (Section 4 ). 3. Evidence from the spectrum. Our spectral diagnostics establish that most singular directions of Muon ’s momentum lie below the noise edge.
